messages.body_plain:
Abstract submission *will close 13 January* for International
Statistical Ecology Conference.  Please visit our website for details of
the conference and other exciting developments.

http://www.ncse.org.uk/isec2010

This conference, held at University of Kent 6-9 July 2010 with this list
of invited speakers:
- Professor Lord Robert May
- Richard Barker
- Carmen Fernandez
- Jeff Laake
- Darryl MacKenzie
- Ken Pollock
- Nigel Yoccoz

In addition to invited and contributed speaker sessions, we will also be
hosting a series of workshops prior to the conference (29 June - 5
July).  Our workshop offerings include:
- Modelling Patterns and Dynamics of Species Occurrence by Darryl
MacKenzie (4 days)
- Spatially explicit capture-recapture with R by Murray Efford and David
Borchers (2 days)
- AD Model Builder by Mark Maunder and Anders Nielsen (1 day)
- Open-population capture-recapture and stopover duration models by
Shirley Pledger, Eleni Matechou and Murray Efford (1 day)
These workshops have special pricing for conference participants.

The important dates for the conference are:
- Abstract submission deadline 13 January 2010
- Notification of acceptance 17 February 2010
- Applications for bursaries (developing countries) 1 March 2010
- Early (reduced-cost) registration deadline 31 March 2010

Please visit the website to view details of the conference, speakers,
abstract submission guidelines, excursions, and workshops.  To submit an
abstract, you will need to register on the website to use the abstract
submission feature.  Note that if you were a participant in our 2008
conference, you will *not* need to register a second time for the
website (as our system will remember your username and password).
However, if you cannot remember your username and password, you will
need to register for another username.

We are excited about the upcoming conference and workshop and hope to
see you in Canterbury in July.

--

messages.subject: Re: Long-term monitoring: changing survey effort
messages.body_plain:
Hi Linda:

Regarding your long-term design.  Remember the two aspects to the
estimation of abundance for your marsupials: detection function and
replicate transects.  I appreciate that with endangered species it is
challenging to accumulate sufficient detections to do a good job of
fitting a detection function (that was the purpose of walking transects
multiple times as you note).

On the face of it, you may not need to repeatedly walk transects, as you
propose in your new design. My concern with your proposal however, is
that you ensure you have sufficient detections within a survey window
(which you describe as occurring every year or two), so that you do not
need to pool detections across more than one or two years to fit a
detection function.  As you can guess, if you need to accumulate
sightings over 3 or 4 years to fit your detection function, you need to
assume that the shape of that detection function does not change over
that period of time.  The longer the time needed to accumulate
detections for fitting, the more tenuous the homogeneity of that
function becomes.

I trust you are also going to try to get even spatial coverage in your
surveys henceforth as well.  So I'm afraid you need to incorporate both
adequate spatial coverage *and* sufficient detections for confident
detection function fitting into your future survey protocol.

Hope you find the advice useful.

Reinhold, Linda wrote:
> > There's a pair of islands that are inhabited by four species of endangered marsupials, which we spotlight along 40 pseudo-replicated permanent transects.  It took four trips over two years to build up enough sample sizes of all of the species (each trip alone does not give enough sample sizes for discrete analyses) to get population estimates.  The populations fluctuate in response to rainfall.  I realise we should have done a panel design for these initial surveys to get more even coverage (the animals are more dense in some areas), but too late now.
> > Now we are "monitoring" the islands once every year or two.  This is meant to be the start of an expensive long-term program which will span over decades.  We are going to drop back our survey intensity to walking each transect once instead of the twice it has been the last four trips (this was to bump up the sample sizes).  However, in years with more funding, we may be able to do each transect twice again.  Sometimes transects are missed entirely (or only done once) anyway because we cannot access them in rough weather.
> > I'm guessing it is okay to drop back the effort to doing each transect once for long-term monitoring (from pp.75 and 107 of Advanced DS).
> > Is there then any point in doing each transect twice in those years when we happen to get lots of funding?

messages.body_plain:
Linda,

I work with songbirds at Mississippi State University, and this question
somewhat pertains to some datasets that I am working with. Because our
sampling window for breeding season birds is limited, we often need to
pool years to increase the number of detections.  I have been comparing
models with and without using year as a covariate. I checked with Eric
first and he confirmed this is an appropriate strategy.  Eric stated
"The hope is that yearly variation in detectability is modelled by the
covariate, rather than being absorbed into density".

Hope this helps and thanks again Eric for your help.

messages.subject_clean: hazard rate parameters are highly correlated
messages.body_plain:
Hi Lindesey, list,

Simple answer: so long as the fit looks sensible and the correlation is
not 1 then it is probably nothing to worry about.  Otherwise you may
want to try setting start values or constraining the parameters to help
it produce a sensible fit.  If your data are "gnarly" in some way, you
may want to avoid the hazard rate.

Longer answer: Distance fits the detection function models by maximum
likelihood.  The hazard rate has two parameters: one governing shape and
one scale (see Fig 2.6 of the Intro book).  So, you can think of a 3-d
plot with shape and scale on the x and y axis and likelihood (actually
log likelihood) on the z axis.  Distance attempts to find the top of the
hill -- the highest point on the z axis, and then reports the values of
the shape and scale parameter at that point.  For some data, the hill
shows a strong ridge along the top, rather than a point.  This is an
indication that the parameters are correlated.  If the correlation is
perfect (i.e., 1) then only a linear combination of shape and scale are
identifiable, and not each individual parameter separately.  Then,
variance on the estimate of f(0) would likely blow up.  However, this
rarely (ever?) happens in Distance for the hazard rate model with no
covariates.  Distance warns you when the correlation is very high
(>0.999 I think).  This is because when correlation is high, it may have
trouble finding the top of the ridge, and hence identifying values for
the parameters.  (You can check the estimated correlation on the
Detection Fct/Global/Parameter Estimates page of output at the bottom.)
  So, ask yourself if the fitted function it came up with looks sensible
and fits the data well.  If not, it may be that Distance failed to find
the maximum, so perhaps manually choosing start values may help, if you
can think of sensible start points; also constraining the parameter
values can help (e.g., constraining the scale parameter between so it
can not get too high).  Distance sometimes has trouble fitting hazard
rate functions to very spiked data, when the shape parameter is
estimated to be at, or close to 1 (the lower bound set by default for
this parameter).  If you have spiked data, you need to ask the usual
question about why you have this and what kind of a fit you want (I
expect his has been discussed before on the list).  If you have a small
dataset and this is happening (I'm not sure why it would, however), you
may want to avoid the hazard rate function completely and stick with 1
parameter models if you think they can adequately represent the true
detection function shape.

Hope this helps.  If this doesn't make sense given your data then please
send me your project (zipped up using File | Export) and I'll check it
out.  If others have insights on high correlation please feel free to
chip in!

  - len

messages.subject: density covariates
messages.body_plain:
I am analyzing line transect data collected in seven regions of a
large study area. The main goal of the project is to investigate
which factors affect density of different species. Possible factors
are hunting pressure, distance to road and vegetation. Unfortunately,
for most species encounter rates are fairly low so that I need to use
a global detection function. From what I read in this list and in the
literature this makes a statistical comparison of densities quite
complicated (need for bootstrapping etc.). Royle et. al (2004)
proposed a model that allows covariates for abundance/density and
this was recently implemented in the R package "unmarked". I run a
test dataset with that package and results with covariates on density
are fairly similar to results from Distance with stratification. The
big advantage I see is that I should be able to use a model selection
approach based on AIC to see which model best fits the data.

My main question is if this approach is valid for my question and if
there are any pitfalls I should be aware of.

Thanks,

Mathias

messages.subject: Re: density covariates
messages.body_plain:
I've not used the software but in principal it is fine. Only pitfall is
the assumed Poisson distribution.  Using covariates  for density means
that it is fitting an inhomogeneous Poisson process (IPP) and that can
absorb some variation in density but it is likely that there is still
over-dispersion which means that std errors for density and abundance
may be underestimated.  I haven't widely broadcast it, but there is a
pacakge called DSpat on CRAN that fits IPPs for distance sampling but it
does so using point data.  It works for nice sampling regimes with
rectangular non-overlapping transects but it needs some more coding to
be useful for most practical situations.  It works with grids whereas I
believe unmarked would work at a transect level.  That would be most
useful for point transects where the entire circle is probably in the
same habitat. Lines are more likely to sample a gradient of features.  I
believe the Royle article used point data.  That's my 2 cents.  --jeff
